paragraphs.heading: Two rivers, a long story
paragraphs.text: China's history stretches over thousands of years and a very wide area. Its civilization grew up in the basins of the Yellow River and the Yangtze River. From there it became one of the oldest cradles of civilization in the world.

paragraphs.heading: The first humans
paragraphs.text: An early human species called Homo erectus reached Eurasia between 1.3 and 1.8 million years ago, and many of its remains have turned up in China. The oldest is Yuanmou Man from Yunnan in the southwest, dated to about 1.7 million years ago. The better-known Peking Man, found in Zhoukoudian cave near Beijing, lived between 700,000 and 400,000 years ago, and scrapers and choppers lay with him. The earliest modern humans in China date to between 120,000 and 80,000 years ago, judged from fossil teeth in Fuyan Cave in Hunan.

paragraphs.heading: Farming villages
paragraphs.text: The Neolithic, the stage marked by farming, began in China about 10,000 years ago, though it started at different times in different regions. The oldest cultivated rice, found by the Yangtze, has been carbon-dated to 8,000 years ago. Millet was being farmed in the Yellow River valley by about 7000 BC. Jiahu, lived in from 7000 to 5800 BC, is one of the best preserved early farming villages. Farming brought more people, a way to store and share out crops, and the chance to support skilled craftsmen and officials.

paragraphs.heading: Cultures, crops and animals
paragraphs.text: In the central Yellow River valley, the Yangshao culture lasted from 5000 to 3000 BC and the Longshan culture from 3000 to 2000 BC. Pigs and dogs were the first animals tamed in the region. After about 3000 BC, tame cattle and sheep came in from Western Asia, along with wheat, which stayed a minor crop. Peaches, cherries, oranges, chickens and many vegetables were also domesticated in Neolithic China.

paragraphs.heading: Marks before writing
paragraphs.text: People left symbols that are sometimes called proto-writing, found at Jiahu from around 7000 BC, Damaidi from around 6000 BC, Dadiwan and Banpo. At Damaidi in Ningxia, 3,172 cliff carvings from 6000 to 5000 BC have been found. They show 8,453 individual characters, such as the sun, moon and stars, gods, and scenes of hunting or herding.

paragraphs.heading: The Bronze Age
paragraphs.text: Bronze objects have been found at a site of the Majiayao culture, dated between 3100 and 2700 BC. The Bronze Age also shows up in the Lower Xiajiadian culture of northeast China, from 2200 to 1600 BC. Sanxingdui, in what is now Sichuan, is thought to have been a major city of a Bronze Age culture nobody knew about before, dating from 2000 to 1200 BC. It was first found in 1929 and found again in 1986, and Chinese archaeologists link it to the state of Shu.

paragraphs.heading: The first dynasties
paragraphs.text: The earliest confirmed historical period starts with the Shang dynasty, around 1250 BC, which left the oldest oracle bone inscriptions that survive. The Zhou dynasty followed, from about 1046 to 256 BC. It brought in the Mandate of Heaven and laid the groundwork for Confucianism, Taoism and Legalism. In 221 BC Qin Shi Huang united China for the first time under one central imperial state. The Han dynasty that came next, from 202 BC to 220 AD, built a lasting imperial order, made Confucianism official and encouraged inventions such as paper-making.
